register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Honolulu, the feather lei course
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; her curriculum vitae gives no month
stops.campa: At Na Lima Mili Hulu No'eau in Honolulu she completes the coursework in Hawaiian traditional feather lei making, the first entry her own curriculum vitae records. The craft is a counted one: feathers laid in sequence, each knot holding the last, the finished lei worn rather than hung. She is not yet a Philadelphia teacher and not yet a maker of presidential flags. She is a student, and this is the first certificate in a run of them that crosses four continents inside fifteen years.
suggested_refs: Na Lima Mili Hulu No'eau, Honolulu, the feather-lei school of Aunty Mary Louise Kekuewa

stops.name: Sigtuna, the leather certificate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In June she takes a certificate at Lottas Garfveri in Sigtuna, the old Swedish town on Lake Malaren. Her curriculum vitae records the trade as leather making and adds one word of its own: mastered. A later summary of her training will call it fish-leather tanning; no source she has published carries that phrase. She is learning the hide before she learns the cloth. Every ceremonial apron in the tradition she will one day teach begins as a skin, white lambskin, cut and dressed by a tanner nobody names.
stops.quote: Lottas Garfveri, Sigtuna, Sweden (June 2010) — Certificate. Leather making. Mastered.
suggested_refs: Lottas Garfveri, Sigtuna, working tannery and teaching workshop

stops.name: Seoul, the Han Sang Soo middle course
stops.date_confidence: attested; the course runs January to September 2011
stops.campa: For nine months she trains under a master embroiderer at the Han Sang Soo Embroidery Museum in Seoul and earns the certificate of the Korean traditional embroidery middle course. Han Sang Soo holds the state designation for the craft; the middle course is a graded step in a system that grades. The lineage of her stitch is written down here, teacher to student, in a state register kept for the purpose. In Philadelphia she will study aprons whose makers were never written down at all.
suggested_refs: Han Sang Soo Embroidery Museum, Bukchon, Seoul, and the graded Korean traditional embroidery courses

stops.name: Hampton Court, the Royal School of Needlework
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year on one of her two sites; absent from the other
stops.campa: The Royal School of Needlework keeps its apartments at Hampton Court Palace, and there she takes its Certificate and its Diploma, the Diploma with merit. The school was founded in 1872 to hold hand embroidery against the machine, and it stitches the robes of British coronations. She earns its credential in the same years she is sitting in Paris ateliers. Her older portfolio site omits this training entirely; only her current professional record carries it. Two of her own websites disagree about what she has learned.
stops.quote: Certificate & Diploma (with Merit), Royal School of Needlework, Surrey, UK (2012)
suggested_refs: Royal School of Needlework, Hampton Court Palace, Certificate and Diploma syllabus

stops.name: San Francisco, awaiting the arrival of dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: At the French Consulate in San Francisco, with Instituto Conexiones, she performs in a piece directed by Moise Toure, the production titled Awaiting the Arrival of Dawn. Her own curriculum vitae lists it among lectures and exhibitions without distinguishing it from them, and a later reading of that list calls it a lecture. It is not a lecture. She stands on a stage inside a consulate of the French Republic, a needleworker within a theatre piece, and the whole record of it survives as one line of her own typing.
stops.quote: French Consulate, Instituto Conexiones, San Francisco — March 2012. Performance piece for "Awaiting the arrival of Dawn" with Director Moise Toure'.
suggested_refs: Moise Toure and Les Inachevés, the touring production 'Awaiting the Arrival of Dawn'

stops.name: San Francisco, the jeweler's diploma
stops.date_confidence: inferred month; the curriculum vitae gives the year 2012 only
stops.campa: She takes the jewelry technician's diploma at the Revere Academy of Jewelry Arts in San Francisco, the bench school founded by Alan Revere in 1979. Solder, saw, bezel, the setting of a stone. She has now been certified in feather, hide, silk floss and metal within three years, at Honolulu, Sigtuna, Seoul and San Francisco. The certificates come faster than any one practice could absorb them. She is not qualifying for a trade. She is collecting materials, and by September of the same year she is sitting in a Paris atelier.
stops.quote: Apprenticed trained, I have worked as an artist in the US, Thailand, India, South Korea, France, the UK, Spain, and Sweden primarily focused on painting, and textile arts.
suggested_refs: Revere Academy of Jewelry Arts, San Francisco, jewelry technician diploma track

stops.name: Paris, the Ecole Lesage
stops.date_confidence: contested: her older site gives 2012-2014, her current site gives 2013; month inferred
stops.campa: The Ecole Lesage, school of the embroidery house that has supplied Chanel, Schiaparelli and Balenciaga since 1924. Here the Luneville hook is taught, the crochet held beneath the fabric, beads fed blind onto a chain stitch worked from the wrong side. Her older site dates the diploma 2012 to 2014; her current site dates the course to 2013 and names it Haute Couture Embroidery and Beading. Both records are hers and they do not agree, and neither one fixes an exact address for the school.
suggested_refs: Ecole Lesage, Paris, and the Luneville hook curriculum of the Maison Lesage

stops.name: Paris, the gold wire of Atelier Zardosi
stops.date_confidence: attested; the course runs April 2013 to August 2014
stops.campa: From April she enters Atelier Zardosi in Paris for the Indian Embroidery Certificate, sixteen months of it, finishing in August of the following year. Zardozi is the metal-thread work of the Mughal courts, gold and silver wire couched onto velvet and silk, carried from Persia into India and from India back into the Paris ateliers that now teach it. She is in one city, in the same years, learning the French luxury house's hook and the Mughal court's gold wire. Her curriculum vitae writes one word beside each: mastered.
stops.quote: Atelier Zardosi, Paris, France (April 2013 – August 2014) — Indian Embroidery Certificate. Mastered.
suggested_refs: Atelier Zardosi, Paris, Indian metal-thread embroidery certificate

stops.name: Burlingame, the Royal School exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the showing is repeated in 2014, month unrecorded
stops.campa: The Royal School of Needlework shows at Burlingame on the San Francisco peninsula, and her work hangs in it in two consecutive years. She has by now been the school's student in England and its exhibitor in California, the institution and its American satellite. The world she moves through is organised around named schools rather than named artists. In its listings she is a holder of the school's technique, and the work hangs under the school's name rather than her own.
suggested_refs: Royal School of Needlework exhibitions at its Burlingame, California campus, 2013 and 2014

stops.name: San Francisco Bay, the October segment
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: CBS carries a Breast Cancer Awareness segment in the Bay Area in October and she appears in it. Her curriculum vitae records the date to the day, which it does for almost nothing else. It is the first television of her life and it is not about embroidery; it is about a disease, and she is in it as a person before she is in it as a needleworker. Three years later a Philadelphia station will film her again and call her a Flag Lady. The camera reaches her twice on two coasts before any gallery does.
suggested_refs: CBS Bay Area Breast Cancer Awareness coverage, 15 October 2013

stops.name: Phoenix, the Genentech conference
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: She lectures at a Genentech conference in Phoenix in April. The biotechnology company assembles its people in a desert convention hall and a hand embroiderer is put in front of them to speak on craftsmanship. Her own statement holds that every detail, from design and tracing and stitching through to display and lecture, must be of the highest quality; she names lecturing in the same sentence as tracing and stitching. The room she says it in belongs to a company that manufactures molecules by the litre.
stops.quote: Every detail from creating a design, tracing, and stitching, to displaying and lecturing on the value of craftsmanship must be of the highest value and quality.
suggested_refs: Genentech corporate conference programme, Phoenix, April 2014

stops.name: Harrogate, the international centre
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: The Harrogate International Centre in Yorkshire holds the largest stitching show in Britain, and she presents there in September. Harrogate is a spa town; the exhibition halls fill each year with thread merchants, guild stands and demonstrators working in public. Within a month she will be inside a United States federal heraldic office behind a security perimeter, working on flags that stand behind a president. Thirty days separate the Yorkshire hall from the Virginia fort.
suggested_refs: Harrogate International Centre, September 2015 stitching exhibition programme

stops.name: Fort Belvoir, the Institute of Heraldry
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the post is held from October 2015 to the present
stops.campa: In October she becomes Senior Hand Embroiderer at the Institute of Heraldry, on Gunston Road at Fort Belvoir in Virginia. The Institute is the heraldic authority of the United States federal government, and she specialises in the official Presidential and Vice Presidential flags and serves as lead docent for the heraldics collections. Her artist bio calls this the prestigious job of presidential hand embroidery and dates it 2015. She names the parent agency as the Defense Logistics Agency; the Institute sits under the Secretary of the Army.
stops.quote: Senior Hand Embroiderer | Institute of Heraldry, Defense Logistics Agency (Oct 2015–Present)
suggested_refs: The Institute of Heraldry, 9325 Gunston Road, Fort Belvoir, Virginia, and its Presidential flag specifications

stops.name: Philadelphia, Meet the Flag Ladies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only
stops.campa: CBS Channel 3 in Philadelphia, the station KYW, films her for a segment titled Meet the Flag Ladies and interviews her about her embroidery. Her curriculum vitae spells the reporter Pat Galen; the station's reporter of that name is Pat Gallen. Philadelphia is the city of Betsy Ross, and a woman who sews flags in it is handed a role the city already has a name for. The interview is an interview. The Betsy Ross framing belongs to the station and to the city, not to her.
stops.quote: CBS Channel 3 — 2016. Meet the "Flag Ladies", Pat Galen. Interview discussing embroidery work.
suggested_refs: KYW-TV Philadelphia, 'Meet the Flag Ladies' segment, 2016

stops.name: San Francisco, the Contemporary Jewish Museum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: She presents at the Contemporary Jewish Museum on Mission Street in San Francisco on the seventeenth of February. Six days later she is standing in a brick house on Arch Street in Philadelphia. The two engagements sit six days and twenty-eight hundred miles apart in a single column of her curriculum vitae, one line and then another. That column has no mark for distance and none for kind: lectures, performances, exhibitions and certificates run down it together.
suggested_refs: Contemporary Jewish Museum, 736 Mission Street, San Francisco, February 2017 programme

stops.name: Philadelphia, 250 Years of Flag Making
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Two hundred and thirty-nine Arch Street in Old City, the house where the first flag is said to have been sewn. She exhibits there on the twenty-third of February in a programme titled 250 Years of Flag Making. The Betsy Ross attribution rests on a family account given a century after the fact and is disputed by every historian who has examined it; the house takes its visitors regardless. She exhibits inside the disputed legend, and she exhibits there as a working maker of flags.
stops.quote: Betsy Ross House, Philadelphia — February 23, 2017. 250 Years of Flag making.
suggested_refs: Betsy Ross House, 239 Arch Street, Philadelphia, and the 1870 Canby account of the first flag

stops.name: Marsanne, the paper in the church
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only
stops.campa: The Eglise Saint-Felix at Marsanne, in the Drome, holds a paper installation of hers under the title Same Sky, Meme Ciel. A village church in southern France, a stone shell, and inside it paper rather than thread. Her materials have been widening for a decade: feather, hide, silk floss, gold wire, metal, and now paper. Her statement will later name paper first among the vessels through which narratives unfold. Marsanne has some twelve hundred inhabitants and no gallery. The church is the gallery.
stops.quote: Paper, fabric, and thread become the vessels through which narratives unfold, each piece a page in a book, each shape a moving image.
stops.quote_source: Artist Statement, A.I.R. Gallery artist page, airgallery.org
suggested_refs: Eglise Saint-Felix, Marsanne (Drome), 'Same Sky / Meme Ciel' installation, 2021

stops.name: San Francisco, the Jones Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month inferred to place it after Marsanne
stops.campa: The same paper installation, under the same title, Same Sky, Meme Ciel, is shown at the Jones Institute in San Francisco in the same year. One project across two hemispheres of her working life, the French village and the California city, and her curriculum vitae lists them as separate lines. A reader of that list takes them for two unrelated showings. They are one work under one name, and the ocean between the two showings leaves no mark on the page.
suggested_refs: The Jones Institute, San Francisco, 'Same Sky / Meme Ciel' paper installation, 2021

stops.name: Denton, Materials Hard and Soft
stops.date_confidence: contested: her current site gives 3 February to 6 May 2022, her older bio gives February to May 2023
stops.campa: The Patterson-Appleton Arts Center in Denton, Texas takes her into Materials: Hard and Soft, the international contemporary craft competition the city has run since 1987. Her own bio says roughly eight hundred entries were submitted and hers was chosen, and dates the run February to May 2023; her current professional record dates the same exhibition February to May 2022. Both sources are her own. The eight hundred figure has no source but her, and the conflict between the two dates is left standing rather than resolved.
suggested_refs: Materials: Hard + Soft International Contemporary Craft Competition, Meadows Gallery, Patterson-Appleton Arts Center, Denton

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Masonic Library
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the founding date of the Mason Stitch Art Collective; her own record gives no start date for the post
stops.campa: One North Broad Street, the Masonic Temple of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, and she becomes its hand embroidery teacher and exhibition curator, founding the Mason Stitch Art Collective there. Her students' finished work is shown in the building and much of her own research is done in its reading room. Benjamin Franklin was initiated in this city in 1731 and printed Anderson's Constitutions here in 1734; Prince Hall organised a lodge here under his own warrant in 1797. She now teaches needlework inside the institution that grew from both.
stops.quote: an artist, curator, researcher and teacher of Masonic embroidery in Philadelphia, USA
suggested_refs: Masonic Library and Museum of Pennsylvania, One North Broad Street; the Mason Stitch Art Collective

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Pennant Flag Exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the exhibition runs into 2024
stops.campa: The Delaware River Waterfront Corporation hangs a Pennant Flag Exhibition along the river frontage, and her work is in it into the following year. Flags again, outdoors this time, weathering. She has embroidered the flags that stand behind a president in a windowless federal office and she has hung pennants over the Delaware where the wind takes them apart. The same craft serves the sealed room and the open pier. Philadelphia gives her both inside two miles of each other.
sources: Delaware River Waterfront Corporation exhibition records, via web search summary
suggested_refs: Delaware River Waterfront Corporation, Pennant Flag Exhibition, 2023-2024

stops.name: Amherst, room VA4 at Mount San Angelo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the residency runs 15 to 17 November only
stops.campa: Mount San Angelo, the Virginia Center for the Creative Arts at Amherst, room VA4, three days in November, work titled Transient Nature of Things. Not an open-ended residency: the fifteenth to the seventeenth, and her own record gives the room number. She is fifty miles from the Blue Ridge and a hundred and fifty from the Institute of Heraldry where she is employed. The title is her own. Thread, paper and hide all fail in time, and so do the attributions attached to old cloth.
sources: Virginia Center for the Creative Arts residency records, via web search summary
suggested_refs: Virginia Center for the Creative Arts, 154 San Angelo Drive, Amherst, Virginia

stops.name: Philadelphia, Process-Based Art
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of December the Masonic Temple shows Process-Based Art, and her work is in it, in the building where she teaches. Process rather than object: the tracing, the frame, the counted hours. Her statement puts design, tracing, stitching, display and lecturing on one level of quality, and a process exhibition takes her at her word. The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania has mounted exhibitions of its own collections for a century. It now mounts one of the work its own classroom produced.
suggested_refs: 'Process-Based Art', Masonic Temple, Philadelphia, 16 December 2023

stops.name: London, the unstitched coif
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by her own record; the accession prefix T.99-2024 fixes the year
stops.campa: The Victoria and Albert Museum accessions T.99-2024 in January: an unstitched coif, made in the United States in 2023, linen with cotton thread and glass beads, hand embroidery with painting and staining, entered in the Textiles and Fashion Collection and held in store at South Kensington. The maker is recorded as Duwenavue Sante Johnson. It is the only object under her name in the museum's catalogue. A coif is a close-fitting cap. An unstitched coif is a coif undone, and the title is hers.
stops.quote: an unstitched coif . . .
stops.quote_source: Victoria and Albert Museum, object title, accession T.99-2024
suggested_refs: V&A accession T.99-2024, Textiles and Fashion Collection, South Kensington store

stops.name: Philadelphia, the apron in the case
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the corpus does not date her study of the object, and the pin is inherited from madame_de_lafayette.journey.json
stops.campa: In a case at One North Broad Street lies a Masonic apron of silk, and the tradition attached to it says Madame de Lafayette embroidered it and that it was presented to General Washington in 1771. Washington is not a general until 1775. Lafayette is eleven in 1771 and has not met him. Adrienne de Noailles does not marry Lafayette until 1774. The museum's own account says only that the apron was thought to be made for Washington and reached the Grand Lodge in 1829. The popular retelling states the 1771 date without qualification.
stops.quote: This cannot be documented as fact
stops.quote_source: Masonic Temple, Library and Museum of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, quoted in madame_de_lafayette.journey.json
suggested_refs: Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania museum record for the apron transferred by the Washington Benevolent Society, 3 July 1829

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the apron from the other end
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no source places her here; the pin is inherited from george_washington.journey.json
stops.campa: Mount Vernon on the Potomac, the estate and the papers. This apron is narrated from the other end here too: in George Washington's own papers it is called the Marques de Lafayette apron, carried to him by John Rutledge Junior, with the note that the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania afterwards withdrew the attribution in its own museum record. The tradition of its making in Paris credits Madame de Lafayette by name. Johnson works in the building that holds the object and disputes the label. No record places her at Mount Vernon itself; the crossing belongs to the object, not to her.
suggested_refs: Mount Vernon Ladies' Association collections and the Washington papers

stops.name: Fredericksburg, the attested initiation
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the 4 November 1752 initiation is lodge-attested, but no source places Johnson in Virginia for it
stops.campa: Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4, where Washington was initiated an Entered Apprentice on the fourth of November 1752. The lodge minutes attest the initiation. Almost everything later hung upon it, the aprons above all, is not attested at all. Johnson teaches the history of those aprons inside a Grand Lodge museum, which is to say she teaches on both sides of that line: the attested initiation and the unattested legend built up around it, the same kind of legend the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania's own museum has quietly withdrawn attributions for before.
suggested_refs: Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4 minute books, November 1752

stops.name: Philadelphia, the canonical Masonic pin
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the pin is inherited byte-identical from benjamin_franklin.journey.json and prince_hall.journey.json
stops.campa: One North Broad Street sits inside the same Masonic Philadelphia that Benjamin Franklin and Prince Hall both built. Franklin is initiated at St John's Lodge in 1731 and prints Anderson's Constitutions in this city in 1734. Prince Hall organises a lodge here under his own warrant on the twenty-second of March 1797. The Grand Lodge that grew out of those acts holds the apron Johnson studies and employs her to teach the needlework it was made with. Two hundred and ninety years of this city's Masonic record sit within walking distance of her classroom.
suggested_refs: St John's Lodge, Philadelphia; Anderson's Constitutions, printed by Franklin, 1734

stops.name: Tyre, the craftsman's harbour
stops.date_confidence: legendary: narrative time only, pin inherited byte-identical from hiram_abiff.journey.json
stops.campa: Tyre on the Phoenician coast, traditionally named as the birthplace of Hiram Abiff, the bronze-caster whose murder and raising supply the whole symbolic vocabulary of the lodge: the lambskin, the working tools, the apron's flap and its strings. The craft Johnson teaches at One North Broad Street draws its iconography from a legend about a workman out of this harbour. The line from Tyre to a Philadelphia classroom is genealogical and not documentary, a lineage of symbol rather than a chain of evidence.
suggested_refs: The Hiramic legend in the third degree ritual; Tyre in 1 Kings 7

stops.name: Jerusalem, the workman's lambskin
stops.date_confidence: legendary: narrative time only, canonical Temple Mount pin inherited from the corpus
stops.campa: The Temple Mount, where the operative masons' white lambskin apron is traced by the craft's own account. Hiram Abiff is murdered at the temple in the legend every lodge reenacts, and the apron is the garment of that reenactment. Johnson teaches this lineage as part of the apron's history: the Solomonic workman's leather, and beside it the embroidered girdle of the Kohanim that Exodus specifies at chapters twenty-eight and thirty-nine. Neither is a place she has stood. Both are places the object she curates claims.
suggested_refs: Exodus 28 and 39 on the embroidered girdle of the Kohanim; the Masonic lecture on the lambskin apron

stops.name: Paris, the rue de Bourbon house
stops.date_confidence: traditional; canonical Paris pin, the exact townhouse not fixed by sources
stops.campa: The rue de Bourbon house in Paris, where Madame de Lafayette is said to have embroidered the apron, the rare case in this whole tradition where the maker is a named woman rather than an unsigned hand. Every other apron in the tradition arrives at the case unsigned. Johnson's own reading of the Masonic archive is that lodge records kept the chain of owners meticulously while the woman who made the object went unrecorded. Here a name survives, and the museum still doubts it.
stops.quote: secret stitches on the reverse side or hidden in plain view
suggested_refs: The Lafayette residence on the rue de Bourbon, Paris, 1784

stops.name: Budapest, the properties seized
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the corpus; the city pin is the atlas's own localization of a country-level statement
stops.campa: Masonic properties are seized across Hungary in 1919 under the dictatorship of the proletariat, and the lodges are outlawed by the fascist counter-revolution the following year. The record states it at the level of the whole country rather than any single city. What is seized is not only buildings. Aprons, collars and banners go with them, all of it hand embroidered, all of it inventoried by the people taking it, the same kind of object Johnson later curates and teaches from in Philadelphia.
suggested_refs: Hungarian lodge seizures of 1919 and the 1920 prohibition

stops.name: Berlin, the Anti-Masonic Exposition
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the venue is not named in the source
stops.campa: In 1934 the Reich Ministry of the Interior dissolves every Masonic lodge in Germany. In 1937 Joseph Goebbels inaugurates the first Anti-Masonic Exposition. The regalia becomes exhibit material: the apron taken off the brother and hung on a wall as evidence against him. Johnson's research covers what became of Masonic embroidery in the twentieth century, and Berlin is where the cloth changes hands. Her own portfolio also carries a separate and unrelated Berlin project, a page titled Berlin 5x5, distinct from this history and no part of it.
suggested_refs: The 1937 Anti-Masonic Exposition, Berlin; the 1934 Ministry of the Interior dissolution order

stops.name: Belgrade, the largest collection ever assembled
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the venue building is not named in the source and the atlas has not located it
stops.campa: The Grand Anti-Masonic Exhibition of 1941 opens in occupied Belgrade, and the essay calls it the largest collection of Masonic embroideries in history. The aprons of a continent, looted lodge by lodge, hung together for the first and only time by the people who took them. The venue itself is not named in any source reached. Johnson's own research traces what became of Masonic embroidery across exactly this stretch of the twentieth century, and this exhibition sits inside it. The largest showing of this needlework ever assembled was assembled as an accusation against the people who made it.
stops.quote: This represented the largest collection of Masonic embroideries in history.
suggested_refs: The Grand Anti-Masonic Exhibition, Belgrade, 1941, and its surviving catalogue

stops.name: Wewelsburg, Ideology and Terror
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; the atlas dates it to the opening of the permanent exhibition
stops.campa: The KreisMuseum Wewelsburg, in the triangular castle the SS took for its own, holds a permanent collection titled Ideology and Terror of SS. The record places German artifacts of fascist fabric culture inside it and stops there. Whether looted Masonic embroidery is among them is unconfirmed, an inference rather than a documented fact. Cloth made by hand for one order can end up in the cases of another, and this is the room where that question stands unresolved.
stops.quote: The permanent collection of KreisMuseum Wewelsburg, titled "Ideology and Terror of SS", includes similar German artifacts of fascist fabric culture.
suggested_refs: KreisMuseum Wewelsburg, 'Ideologie und Terror der SS' permanent exhibition

stops.name: Salo, L'ultimo Fascismo
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; the atlas dates it to the opening of the museum's permanent display
stops.campa: At the Museo di Salo on Lake Garda the exhibit L'ultimo Fascismo: La Repubblica Sociale Italiana presents the material culture of Mussolini's last republic, hand embroidered flags among it and the details of military uniforms. Not Masonic textiles here but the fabric of the regime that banned them: Italy forbade co-membership in the lodges and the party in 1924 and disbanded the order the year after. The same needle serves the fraternity and the state that outlaws it. The essay places both in one paragraph.
stops.quote: The exhibit at the Museo di Salò, titled "L'ultimo Fascismo: La Repubblica Sociale Italiana", presented artifacts of this material culture, including hand embroidered flags and details of military uniforms.
suggested_refs: MuSa, Museo di Salo, Via Brunati 9, and the Repubblica Sociale Italiana display

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Mural Arts fellowship
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Mural Arts Philadelphia names her a Black Fellow in March. It is a fellowship and not representation, and the distinction matters because a summary of her affiliations will call it representation. Mural Arts is the largest public art programme in the United States and it works on the sides of buildings; she works at a scale of millimetres. The city that filmed her as a Flag Lady in 2016 and gave her a Masonic classroom in 2022 now funds her under a third heading.
suggested_refs: Mural Arts Philadelphia Black Artist Fellowship, March 2024 cohort

stops.name: Jenkintown, the Spring Solo Series
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the venue; her own curriculum vitae dates it loosely April 2023 to April 2024
stops.campa: The Abington Art Center on Meetinghouse Road at Jenkintown gives her the Spring Solo Series, on view from the twenty-seventh of April to the thirty-first of May. Her own curriculum vitae dates the show loosely, April 2023 to April 2024, though the venue's own listing gives the exact dates above. It is her first solo exhibition in the Philadelphia region. The work is hers alone on the walls with no school's name above it, fifteen years after the first certificate at Honolulu.
suggested_refs: Abington Art Center, 515 Meetinghouse Road, Jenkintown, Solo Series Spring 2024

stops.name: Manchester, the first degree
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by two independent records
stops.campa: Southern New Hampshire University confers the Bachelor of Arts in Communication Arts in May. She is by then a federal heraldic embroiderer, a Grand Lodge curator, a fellow of Mural Arts and the maker of an accessioned object in the Victoria and Albert. The degree comes last and it is not in art. The university sits at Hooksett rather than Manchester and the study was in all likelihood online. A woman certified in six countries takes her first academic degree.
suggested_refs: Southern New Hampshire University, BA Communication Arts, May 2025

stops.name: Brooklyn, Quiet Observations
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the term membership runs 2024 to 2030
stops.campa: A.I.R. Gallery in DUMBO, Brooklyn, the artist-run cooperative founded in 1972 as the first all-women gallery in the United States. She is a National Member on a term running 2024 to 2030, and from the ninth of August to the seventh of September her solo exhibition Quiet Observations shows recent hand embroidery, collage and painting on history, time, memory, balance and stillness. The artist statement that hangs with it is the statement her older portfolio site has never carried.
stops.quote: Like a china cabinet falling to the ground, I collect and sort through retrievable pieces of fragments, each containing a seeded memory.

stops.name: Philadelphia, the micro-grant at Cherry Street Pier
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season only: Winter 2025
stops.campa: The Bartol Foundation names her the Winter 2025 recipient of the Marrazzo Teaching Artist Micro-Grant, funding community workshops at Cherry Street Pier that take the stories of individual narrators and work them into a single unified textile. Many hands to one cloth is how the aprons in her museum were made, and the makers' names are the part the lodge records left out. On the pier the narrators keep their names, the workshops are public, and the grant is issued to a teaching artist the foundation names in full.
stops.quote: My mission is to engage audiences and promote dialogue, understanding, and appreciation of our diverse heritage and shared history.
stops.quote_source: Artist Statement, A.I.R. Gallery artist page, airgallery.org

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Historical Society and Francis Johnson
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only
stops.campa: The Historical Society of Pennsylvania on Locust Street, where she researches the Philadelphia composer Francis Johnson for the project Changing Faces of Independence and turns his musical legacy into embroidered work. The resulting piece, Arrival: Musical Soiree, enters the Society's permanent collection. Francis Johnson led the first Black band to perform for European royalty and died in this city in 1844. She shares his surname and no established descent, a coincidence the record notes without claiming anything more from it.

stops.name: Philadelphia, Landed Sky
stops.date_confidence: contested: registry listing gives March to May 2026, the gallery's own site carried no listing when checked
stops.campa: Tiger Strikes Asteroid Philadelphia, the artist-run gallery whose Secretary she has been since 2021, shows her solo exhibition How will our Ancestors find us?: Landed Sky from March to May. The gallery's own site does not list the show, and the title rests on secondary sourcing rather than a primary announcement. She is exhibiting in a room she helps govern, which is what artist-run means and is not what an invitation means. The same distinction holds here as it holds between a fellowship and representation.
stops.quote: My current body of work, "Things Falling Apart and Break Away Migrations," explores the concept of retrieval and transformation.
stops.quote_source: Artist Statement, A.I.R. Gallery artist page, airgallery.org

stops.name: Philadelphia, How Water Moves
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month inferred, and the venue's own events page carried no listing when checked
stops.campa: Cherry Street Pier at 121 North Columbus Boulevard, where she co-curates How Water Moves: Language and the Tactile. Co-curator and not curator; the venue's own events page carries no listing for it. She is alive, working, and has no tomb, no grave, no plaque and no monument. The nearest thing to a memorial in her whole record is a silk apron in a case at One North Broad Street which commemorates somebody else and may not have been made by the woman whose name it carries.
stops.quote: I aim to inspire others to embrace their roots and diversity, fostering understanding and connection through visual art and techniques like hand embroidery.
stops.quote_source: Artist Statement, A.I.R. Gallery artist page, airgallery.org
